sweep_summary: Erzya (erzy1239) is in the catalog as fixed-strict initial on a third-hand chain (Walker < Kenstowicz < Tsygankin & Debaev 1975, not located). Both works with stress in the title are print-only SUST monographs (Estill 2004, SUST 246; Lehiste et al. 2003, SUST 245): not on edition.fi (SUST catalog pages 1-3 checked, 245-246 absent), not in Helda/Tartu dspace/archive.org, Google Books no preview (snippets only). But Estill's own 3-page lectio praecursoria summarising the 2004 monograph is open on journal.fi (Virittäjä 109/1, 2005) and was downloaded and read: present-day stress is predominantly on the first syllable (in 1785/1788 documents mostly on the second), yet 'the position of word stress is not structurally determined, and the speaker may, in general, stress any syllable desired' ('preferential' stress); disyllables somewhat regularly initial, polysyllables evenly distributed, lists read with initial stress. This is corroborated by first-hand empirical work already held by the project and read: Aasmäe & Ross 2005 (57% initial, 30% non-initial, 13% double in spontaneous speech of 33 speakers; idiolect-dependent), Aasmäe 2006 PhD (initial prevails in reading and in reduction dialects; literary handbooks incl. Devayev & Tsygankin 1970: 76 call stress free), Aasmäe 2015 (Paasonen: Erzya stress free/not fixed; today initial dominant only in dialect groups 3-4), Aasmäe 2014: 13 (typically odd-numbered syllables, movable by sentence rhythm) and Rueter 2010: 14 ('virtually free word stress'). Net: the 'fixed' part of fixed-strict is contradicted by every first-hand source; 'initial' stands only as the statistically dominant pattern. Lehiste et al. 2003 remains unread (snippets: 'words were perceived as stressed on the first syllable'; non-initial stress tied to low a/ä in non-initial syllables; Aasmäe 2006: 23 cites pp. 50, 86 for initial stress in script reading) — high acquisition priority, as is the Estill 2004 monograph itself. Also found: Estill's 1995 and 1997 Helsinki theses (Helda metadata only), his 2000 CIFU abstract, and Keresztes's 2005 FUD review (all print-only, low priority).

new_statements.quote: As far as the next matter is concerned, it must be said that although Erzya word stress has earlier generally been on the second syllable, and nowadays it is predominantly on the first syllable, the analysed material clearly demonstrates how then and now the speaker is free to place stress in accordance with personal preferences. The position of word stress is not structurally determined, and the speaker may, in general, stress any syllable desired. In this respect, Erzya is something of an exceptional language.
new_statements.citation: Estill, Dennis. 2005. Diachronic change in Erzya word stress [Lectio praecursoria, University of Helsinki, 22 Nov 2004; author's summary of SUST 246]. Virittäjä 109(1), verkkoliite, 3 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 2, second paragraph (also p. 1 for the 1785/1788 vs present-day result)
new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the author of the only monograph devoted to Erzya word stress: present-day Erzya stress is predominantly word-initial as a statistical fact (disyllables 'somewhat regularly initially stressed', lists read with initial stress), but placement is not structurally fixed — 'preferential', speaker-determined, mobile over any syllable, with polysyllables 'rather evenly distributed'. This agrees with the on-disk empirical work of Aasmäe (2005 with Ross: 57% initial / 30% non-initial / 13% double in spontaneous speech; 2006; 2015: initial stress dominant only in the vowel-reduction dialects, alternation high in the full-vowel dialects) and with Paasonen's original 'not fixed'. The catalog's fixed-strict initial coding rests on a third-hand chain (Walker 1996 < Kenstowicz 1995 < Tsygankin & Debaev 1975, never located) and is contradicted as a 'fixed' rule; 'initial' survives only as the dominant tendency (reading, reduction dialects, disyllables). Recommended reading: mobile/free stress with a strong initial preference, lexical_stress disputed as already carried.

sources.citation: Estill, Dennis. 2005. Diachronic change in Erzya word stress [Lectio praecursoria, University of Helsinki, 22 November 2004]. Virittäjä 109(1), verkkoliite (Lektiot), 3 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 1: "An unusual feature of Erzya is its word stress, which differs from at least most other languages insofar as speakers may lay stress on any syllable they wish. It is difficult to fit such word stress into any existing typology. I have called this type of word stress preferential." ... "An analysis of these showed that slightly over two hundred years ago word stress was, for the most part, statistically on the second syllable, whereas today it is on the first syllable with almost the same regularly." p. 2: "The position of word stress is not structurally determined, and the speaker may, in general, stress any syllable desired."
sources.locator: pp. 1-3 (verkkoliite pagination); key statements p. 1 (intro, result 1) and p. 2 (result 2), pp. 2-3 (acoustic study)
sources.note: Author's own summary of the 2004 monograph: present-day Erzya stress is predominantly on the first syllable (in the 1785/1788 documents it was mostly on the second), but it is speaker-'preferential', not structurally determined; 'nowadays disyllabic words are somewhat regularly initially stressed, although word stress is rather evenly distributed in the case of polysyllabic words' (pp. 2-3); 'today lists are read with initial stress' (p. 3); intensity and duration matter more than F0 for word stress; no evidence that first-syllable stress is inherited from Proto-Mordvin.

sources.citation: Aasmäe, Niina. 2014. An Introductory Course of the Erzya Language. Tartu: Paul Ariste Centre. (section 'Stress', p. 13)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: "In Erzya, the acoustic properties of stress are relatively weakly expressed, and the place of the stressed syllable in a word may vary. In polysyllabic words, additional stress appears. Typically, stress falls on odd-numbered syllables; for example, in the word śed́ejsenze 'in his/her heart', the first and third syllables receive stress. Sentence rhythm may cause the stress to move to even-numbered syllables. ... Changes in the position of stress do not bring about changes in the meaning of a word."
sources.note: Pedagogical grammar: stress typically on odd-numbered syllables (first and third), movable by sentence rhythm, non-distinctive; Russian loans re-stressed to the first syllable.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: "Erzya is known for its virtually free word stress ... Sentence stress is the predominant cause of stress variation in Erzya words, whereas Erzya words can take main stress on all feet (cf. also Ryabov 1935; Estill 2004)."
sources.locator: p. 14 ('The Erzya literary language of today')
sources.note: Passing statement in a morphology monograph: virtually free word stress, driven by sentence stress; cites Estill 2004.

sources.citation: Aasmäe, Niina. 2015. The observations of Heikki Paasonen concerning word stress in Erzya and Moksha. Suomalais-Ugrilaisen Seuran Aikakauskirja 95: 9-23.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 11: "The well-known statement made by H. Paasonen reads that in Erzya stress is not discernible, while in Moksha it has a clearly expressed effect of prominence (p. 8). H. Paasonen defines the location of stress in both Erzya and Moksha as free ... In Erzya, the location of stress freely alternates in di- and trisyllabic and even in longer words"; p. 12: "In the amendments, Paasonen suggests that words in Erzya do not have fixed stress (p. IX)." p. 14: "In groups 3 and 4, stress was predominantly on the word-initial syllable; in the responses of speaker group 4, the occurrences of stress on the word-initial syllable were the most frequent."
sources.note: Paasonen (1893/1903) described Erzya stress as free/not fixed and indistinct; Aasmäe's present-day data (33 speakers) show four dialect groups: group 1 (Ardatov/Atyashevo, Nizhny Novgorod diaspora, full vowels) with high stress alternation, groups 3-4 (Bolshie Berezniki, Kochkurovo, Torbeyevo; vowel reduction) predominantly word-initial stress with stressed vowels significantly longer.

sources.citation: Aasmäe, Niina. 2006. Stress and Quantity in Erzya. Dissertationes Philologiae Uralicae Universitatis Tartuensis 6. Tartu: Tartu University Press (PhD).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 5: "Data for two idiolect-groups showed a high occurrence of both initial and non-initial stress, while in the other idiolect groups stress was predominantly assigned on the initial syllable." p. 23: "In reading, especially controlled frame sentences, word-initial stress prevails. It has also been mentioned in previous studies of Erzya stress that speakers dominantly located stress on word-initial syllables while reading a script (Lehiste et al. 2003: 50, 86; Estill 2004: 165)." p. 33: "Concerning the standards of literary Erzya, it has been stated that stress is free (Devayev and Tsygankin 1970: 76; Bondarko and Polyakov 1993: 142; Zaicz 1998: 190-191; Bartens 1999: 28)."
sources.note: Word stress is non-distinctive and mobile, assigned to odd- or even-numbered syllables in duple feet that can cross word boundaries ('stress thus appears to be associated with the domain of syntax', p. 18); initial stress prevails in reading and in reduction dialects; literary-language handbooks (incl. Devayev & Tsygankin 1970: 76 — the co-author of the catalog's cited Tsygankin & Debaev 1975) call stress free.

sources.citation: Aasmäe, Niina & Jaan Ross. 2005. How free is alternating stress in Erzya? Linguistica Uralica 41(2): 134-143.

sources.note: Open-access report of the 33-speaker elicitation experiment behind Aasmäe 2006 ch.1.5.2; gives the 57/30/13% initial/non-initial/double split that directly refutes 'uniformly initial'. downloaded now.
